data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's own terms without smuggling in induction, provided it is framed strictly as a methodological rule based on the asymmetry of risk and informational content rather than a prediction of future truth.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly states that choosing a better-corroborated theory for action implies a belief in its higher probability of being true in the future.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the defense requires attributing any pragmatic advantage or predictive reliability to corroboration that functions identically to inductive probability.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If it can be demonstrated that the 'asymmetry of risk' argument secretly assumes the uniformity of nature (that the future will resemble the past).","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Popper distinguishes between the logical status of a theory (which corroboration does not alter regarding probability) and the rational choice of which theory to test or act upon. The mechanism relies on 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) as a regulative ideal and the 'asymmetry of risk': acting on a falsified theory guarantees error, while acting on a severely tested (but not falsified) theory offers the best available, albeit non-probabilistic, guess at closeness to truth. This transforms the preference from an inductive inference about the future to a critical decision procedure grounded in past performance and logical content.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
